url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.content:
**Short answer:** For most applications the *canonical* way to represent currency valuations over time is a **time‑series table** (or a `pandas.DataFrame` / `polars.DataFrame` in memory). If you need to persist it, store it in a relational database (PostgreSQL + TimescaleDB, ClickHouse, etc.) or a dedicated time‑series database (InfluxDB, VictoriaMetrics, QuestDB, etc.). Below I’ll walk through the options, why they’re good, and when you might pick one over another. --- ## 1. In‑memory representation | Structure | Typical use | Pros | Cons | |-----------|-------------|------|------| | **`pandas.DataFrame`** (or `polars`, `vaex`) | Data science, analytics, quick prototyping | • Built‑in datetime index
• Vectorised operations
• Rich ecosystem (plotting, stats, ML)
• Easy to export to CSV/Parquet | • Memory‑heavy for very large series
• Requires Python environment | | **`numpy.ndarray` + separate timestamp array** | High‑performance numeric work | • Very fast numeric ops
• Low memory overhead | • No built‑in time‑indexing
• Manual handling of missing data | | **`dict[datetime, dict[pair, rate]]`** | Small‑scale, flexible lookup | • Fast O(1) lookup by timestamp
• Easy to serialize to JSON | • Inefficient for range queries
• No ordering guarantees | | **`list[tuple[datetime, pair, rate]]`** sorted by datetime | Simple persistence in memory | • Ordered, easy to iterate
• Can binary‑search | • Linear search for exact timestamp
• Manual handling of duplicates | ### Recommendation for in‑memory - **Use a DataFrame** if you plan to do any analytics, resampling, or need to join with other time series. - **Use a dict-of-dicts** if you only need point‑lookup and your dataset is small. - **Use a list of tuples** if you need to keep insertion order and will iterate sequentially. --- ## 2. Persistent storage | Database | Why it’s good for currency time series | Typical schema | Indexing strategy | When to choose | |----------|----------------------------------------|----------------|-------------------|----------------| | **PostgreSQL + TimescaleDB** | Relational + hypertable optimisations | `ts TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, base TEXT, quote TEXT, rate NUMERIC` | Composite index `(ts, base, quote)` | You already use Postgres, need ACID, and want SQL tooling | | **ClickHouse** | Columnar, very fast reads, good for analytics | Same as above | Primary key `(ts, base, quote)` | You need high‑throughput ingestion and analytical queries | | **InfluxDB** | Native time‑series DB, downsampling, retention policies | `measurement="fx", tags={base,quote}, fields={rate}, timestamp` | Tag indexes on `base` & `quote` | You need built‑in retention, continuous queries, or real‑time dashboards | | **TimescaleDB** | Same as Postgres but with time‑series features | Same as above | Composite index `(ts, base, quote)` | You want SQL compatibility + time‑series features | | **QuestDB** | Columnar, high‑write throughput, SQL | Same as above | Primary key `(ts, base, quote)` | You need ultra‑fast ingestion and low latency | | **Redis (sorted sets)** | In‑memory, low latency | `ZADD fx:{base}:{quote} ts rate` | Sorted set per pair | You need sub‑millisecond lookups and can tolerate in‑memory limits | | **MongoDB (time‑series collection)** | Flexible schema, built‑in TS support | `ts, base, quote, rate` | Compound index `(ts, base, quote)` | You need document flexibility and built‑in TS features | | **SQLite** | Lightweight, no server | Same as above | Composite index | You’re building a desktop app or prototype | ### Schema design tips 1. **Composite primary key**: `(ts, base, quote)` ensures uniqueness and allows efficient range scans. 2. **Partitioning / Sharding**: For very large datasets, partition by month/year or shard by currency pair. 3. **Retention policy**: If you only need the last 5 years, set a TTL or delete older rows automatically. 4. **Downsampling**: Store daily averages or OHLCV (open/high/low/close/volume) if you don’t need every tick. 5. **Index on `ts`**: Essential for range queries (`WHERE ts BETWEEN start AND end`). 6. **Index on `base` & `quote`**: Needed for filtering by pair. --- ## 3. Choosing the right tool | Scenario | Recommended tool | Rationale | |----------|------------------|-----------| | **Rapid prototyping / analytics** | `pandas` | Quick to load, transform, plot. | | **Production analytics with SQL** | PostgreSQL + TimescaleDB | ACID, mature tooling, SQL. | | **High‑frequency ingestion + analytics** | ClickHouse / QuestDB | Columnar, fast writes, analytical queries. | | **Real‑time dashboards** | InfluxDB | Built‑in retention, continuous queries, Grafana integration. | | **In‑memory cache** | Redis sorted sets | Sub‑ms lookups, TTL support. | | **NoSQL flexibility** | MongoDB time‑series | Document model, flexible schema. | | **Embedded / offline** | SQLite | Zero‑config, portable. | --- ## 4. Example: PostgreSQL + TimescaleDB ```sql CREATE TABLE fx_rates ( ts TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, base TEXT NOT NULL, quote TEXT NOT NULL, rate DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (ts, base, quote) ); SELECT create_hypertable('fx_rates', 'ts'); -- Index for fast pair lookup CREATE INDEX ON fx_rates (base, quote); ``` Query example: ```sql -- Get EUR/USD rates for the last week SELECT ts, rate FROM fx_rates WHERE base = 'EUR' AND quote = 'USD' AND ts >= now() - INTERVAL '7 days' ORDER BY ts; ``` --- ## 5. Example: InfluxDB ```bash # Write a point curl -i -XPOST http://localhost:8086/write?db=fx \ --data-binary 'fx,base=EUR,quote=USD rate=1.2345 1625097600000000000' # Query curl -i -XPOST http://localhost:8086/query?db=fx \ --data-urlencode "q=SELECT rate FROM fx WHERE base='EUR' AND quote='USD' AND time > now() - 7d" ``` --- ## 6. Summary | Goal | Best structure | Why | |------|----------------|-----| | **Fast point lookup** | `dict[datetime, dict[pair, rate]]` or Redis sorted set | O(1) access | | **Range queries / analytics** | DataFrame or SQL hypertable | Ordered, vectorised, indexed | | **Very large scale** | ClickHouse / QuestDB | Columnar, compression, fast aggregation | | **Real‑time dashboards** | InfluxDB | Built‑in retention, continuous queries | | **Embedded / offline** | SQLite | Zero‑config, portable | Pick the one that matches your workload: if you’re doing heavy analytics, go with a DataFrame or TimescaleDB; if you need ultra‑fast ingestion, consider ClickHouse or QuestDB; if you’re building a dashboard, InfluxDB is a natural fit.
